To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
forested upstream reach length is the most important factor for the effects of pesticides on macroinvertebrate community composition, followed by the structural quality of the stream channel.
forested upstream areas and riparian buffer zones are the most important factors influencing pesticide effects on macroinvertebrate assemblages.

pesticide exposure is mainly determined by the amount of pesticides applied in the catchment, and that forested upstream areas and riparian buffer zones can mitigate the exposure of aquatic ecosystems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of landscape parameters that can be used to mitigate the effects of pesticides in streams.
the development of an integrative, landscape-based approach to identify sites of concern and to develop mitigation measures.
the development of an integrative and cost-effective approach for the identification of sites at risk of failing the Water Framework Directive objectives due to pesticide exposure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the presence of forested upstream reaches can mitigate the effects of pesticides on macroinvertebrate assemblages and that the presence of riparian buffer strips of at least 5-m width can reduce pesticide exposure.

the presence of diffuse pesticide sources and the lack of forested upstream reaches are the most important landscape parameters for the assessment of pesticide effects on macroinvertebrate community structure.
the pesticide effects on macroinvertebrate community structures are mainly driven by the pesticide exposure and that forested upstream reach can mitigate these effects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pesticide effects can be predicted by a combination of landscape parameters.

forested upstream catchments and riparian buffer zones of at least 5m in width can reduce pesticide effects and exposure in streams and that these landscape elements can be used as mitigation measures.
the effects of pesticides are mitigated if forested upstream reaches are present and if the riparian buffer strip width is 5 m and higher.
The main takeaway from our work is that
landscape parameters can be considered in the assessment of pesticide effects and in the design of mitigation measures.
the effects of pesticides on macroinvertebrate community structure can be predicted using landscape parameters, such as forested upstream reaches or the structural quality of riparian buffer strips.

the mitigation of pesticide pollution is possible and that the implementation of riparian buffer strips and forested upstream areas can contribute to the achievement of the objectives of the Water Directive.
